request.job_description: We are hiring a Data Engineer to own batch and streaming data pipelines and data quality for our analytics and product teams. You will design and operate ingestion and transformation workflows, build reliable streaming jobs, define and enforce data quality checks, and collaborate with analysts and downstream consumers. Experience with Spark, Kafka, SQL, and an orchestration tool such as Airflow is expected, along with strong ownership of production reliability.

transcript.question: Tell me about a batch pipeline you designed and ran in production. What were the key design decisions?
transcript.answer: At my last company I rebuilt our nightly orders pipeline. It was ingesting about 400 GB a day from Postgres replicas and third-party files into S3, then Spark transformations into a warehouse. The old version was a single Airflow DAG that reran everything on failure and took around 7 hours. I split it into partitioned, idempotent tasks keyed by date, used incremental loads based on updated_at watermarks, and added task-level retries with backfill support. Runtime dropped to about 2 hours and reruns of a single day no longer touched other partitions. I was the primary owner and carried the on-call rotation for it. One trade-off was that watermark-based incremental loads miss hard deletes, so we added a weekly full reconciliation job for the key tables.

transcript.question: How have you worked with streaming systems, for example Kafka or Spark Structured Streaming?
transcript.answer: I have used Kafka some. We had a team that produced events to Kafka and I consumed them to land into the data lake. I know about topics and partitions and consumer groups. I haven't really tuned anything myself, I mostly used the connector that was already set up. I think exactly-once is something Kafka supports but I'm not sure how exactly it works.

transcript.question: Describe how you handled a data quality problem. How did you detect it and prevent it from recurring?
transcript.answer: We had an incident where a upstream team changed a currency field from cents to dollars and revenue dashboards were off by 100x for two days before an analyst noticed. After that I added Great Expectations checks on the staging layer: schema checks, null rate thresholds, and range checks on amounts compared against a trailing 14-day distribution. Failing checks block the downstream tasks and page the on-call. I also set up a data contract conversation with the upstream team so schema changes are announced in advance. In the following quarter we caught three bad loads before they reached dashboards, and false-positive alerts were about one a week, which we tuned down by adjusting thresholds.

transcript.question: Tell me about a time you had to explain a pipeline issue or delay to non-technical stakeholders.
transcript.answer: Usually I just tell them it's being fixed and that we will update them. I try to keep it short. Mostly the manager handled the communication with the business teams so I didn't do that much of it directly.

transcript.question: If a streaming job starts lagging behind and consumer lag keeps growing, how would you troubleshoot it?
transcript.answer: I would first look at whether the lag is on all partitions or just a few, since a few could mean a hot key or skew. Then I'd check if the processing time per batch has increased, maybe because of a slow sink or a downstream database. I'd probably scale up the consumers or add resources. I haven't done this in production on my own, but that is what I would try.
